name: Ludwig van Beethoven
info: Ludwig van Beethoven (1770–1827) was a German composer and pianist, born in Bonn and based in Vienna from 1792, whose symphonies, piano sonatas and string quartets carried music from the Classical style toward the Romantic, much of it written as his hearing failed.

facts.born: Baptised on 17 December 1770 at the Catholic parish of St. Remigius in Bonn; the birth date is not documented, though there is a consensus, with which Beethoven himself agreed, that it was 16 December; son of Johann van Beethoven, a court tenor, and Maria Magdalena Keverich
facts.died: 26 March 1827 in Vienna, aged 56, after several months of illness; buried in the Währing cemetery after a funeral procession on 29 March attended by an estimated 10,000 people, and reinterred in 1888 at Vienna's Zentralfriedhof
facts.role: Court organist at Bonn under Elector Maximilian Franz; from 1792 a composer and piano virtuoso in Vienna, supported by noble patrons including Prince Lichnowsky, Prince Lobkowitz and Archduke Rudolf; composer in residence at the Theater an der Wien (1803–1804)
facts.known: nine symphonies, including the Eroica, the Fifth and the Ninth; piano sonatas, among them the Pathétique, the Moonlight and the Hammerklavier; the string quartets, including the late quartets and the Große Fuge; the opera Fidelio; the Missa solemnis; the Diabelli Variations; composing through progressive deafness

t: Born in Bonn into a musical family with an alcoholic father, Beethoven moved to Vienna in 1792, studied with Haydn and became known first as a piano virtuoso and improviser in the salons of the nobility.

From about 1798 his hearing declined, and in 1802 he wrote the Heiligenstadt Testament, recording thoughts of suicide and his resolution to go on living for his art; he never became totally deaf, but by 1818 he and his visitors were writing their conversations in notebooks.

His last years brought the Missa solemnis, the Ninth Symphony, the Diabelli Variations and the late quartets, alongside a bitter legal contest with his sister-in-law over his nephew Karl, who attempted suicide in 1826.
dyk: Beethoven learned to add but never to divide or multiply, and all his life he multiplied by addition, for instance adding up a column of sixteen sevens rather than working out 16 × 7.
ev: Baptised at St. Remigius in Bonn on 17 December; the date of his birth is not documented
Moves permanently to Vienna in November to study with Joseph Haydn, as news arrives that his father has died
Makes his public debut in Vienna over three days, beginning on 29 March at the Burgtheater, and arranges publication of the three piano trios of Opus 1
Writes the Heiligenstadt Testament at Heiligenstadt, recording his thoughts of suicide because of his growing deafness
The Eroica Symphony premieres in early 1805, and Fidelio, in its first version, opens in November to nearly empty houses
Gives a benefit concert in December that premieres the Fifth and Sixth symphonies, the Fourth Piano Concerto and the Choral Fantasy
The Ninth Symphony, with sections of the Missa solemnis, is first performed on 7 May at the Kärntnertortheater
Dies in Vienna on 26 March; about 10,000 people attend the funeral procession three days later

sections.early:
Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn, at what is now the Beethoven House Museum. No authentic record of his birth survives, but the register of his baptism at St. Remigius on 17 December 1770 does, and local custom was to baptise within 24 hours; there is a consensus, with which Beethoven himself agreed, that he was born on 16 December. His grandfather, also Ludwig van Beethoven, had come from Mechelen and risen to be Kapellmeister at the court of the Archbishop-Elector of Cologne. His father Johann was a tenor in the same establishment. Of the seven children born to Johann, only Ludwig and two younger brothers, Kaspar Anton Karl and Nikolaus Johann, survived infancy.

Johann was his first music teacher, from his fifth year, and the regime was harsh and intensive, often reducing the boy to tears. Aware of Leopold Mozart's success with his children, Johann tried to promote his son as a prodigy, claiming on the posters for his first public performance in March 1778 that Ludwig was six; he was seven. From 1780 or 1781 his most important teacher was Christian Gottlob Neefe, who taught him composition, and in March 1783 his first published work, a set of keyboard variations, appeared. He became assistant organist, at first unpaid and from 1784 paid.

The widowed Helene von Breuning became a second mother to him and offered a retreat from a home dominated by Johann's decline through alcoholism. In 1789 Johann was forced to retire from court service and half his pension was ordered paid to Ludwig for the family's support. His mother had died in July 1787.
sections.rise:
Beethoven first met Joseph Haydn in Bonn in December 1790, and again in July 1792 when Haydn was returning from London. Arrangements were likely made then for him to study with Haydn, and Count Waldstein wrote to him: "With the help of assiduous labour you shall receive Mozart's spirit from Haydn's hands." Elector Maximilian Franz had appointed him court organist and helped pay for the move. In November 1792 Beethoven left Bonn for Vienna, amid rumours of war spilling out of France. Shortly afterwards he learned that his father had died.

In Vienna he studied counterpoint with Haydn and later with Johann Albrechtsberger, took violin lessons from Ignaz Schuppanzigh and received occasional instruction from Antonio Salieri. When Bonn fell to the French in October 1794 his stipend effectively ended, but Viennese noblemen, among them Prince Lobkowitz, Prince Karl Lichnowsky and Baron Gottfried van Swieten, had offered him support. By 1793 he had a reputation as a piano virtuoso. He made his public debut in March 1795, and the three Piano Trios of Opus 1, dedicated to Lichnowsky, were a financial success whose profits nearly covered his living expenses for a year.

In 1799 he won a piano duel against Joseph Wölfl, and in 1800 another against Daniel Steibelt. On 2 April 1800 he hired the Burgtheater for a concert that included the premiere of his First Symphony. By the end of 1800 he and his music were in demand from patrons and publishers.
sections.deeds:
Beethoven told the pianist Charles Neate that his hearing loss began in 1798, and by 1801 he was describing his symptoms to friends. The cause was probably otosclerosis, possibly with degeneration of the auditory nerve. On his doctor's advice he stayed at Heiligenstadt from April to October 1802, where he wrote the Heiligenstadt Testament, a letter to his brothers, never sent, that records his thoughts of suicide and his resolve to continue living for and through his art. After it he told Czerny that he intended to take "a new way". The Third Symphony, the Eroica, written in 1803–04, was longer and larger in scope than any earlier symphony. He had titled it "Bonaparte" but, disillusioned when Napoleon declared himself Emperor in 1804, scratched the name from the title page.

The middle period brought the Razumovsky quartets, the Waldstein and Appassionata sonatas, the Violin Concerto, the Fourth to Eighth symphonies and Fidelio, which failed in 1805 and was revised. In 1808 he refused a post as Kapellmeister at Cassel under Napoleon's brother Jérôme after Archduke Rudolf, Prince Kinsky and Prince Lobkowitz pledged him a pension of 4000 florins a year. The concerts of December 1813 and early 1814 around Wellington's Victory and the Seventh Symphony were the most profitable of his career.

He made his last public appearance as a soloist in 1814, and from then on used ear-trumpets and, from about 1818, conversation books.
sections.opponents:
Not every response to his work was admiring. A 1784 review in Forkel's Musikalischer Almanack compared his efforts to those of rank beginners. Haydn believed the third trio of Opus 1 too difficult for an audience to appreciate. The Eroica met a mixed reception in 1805, some listeners objecting to its length or structure. The violinist Felix Radicati said the Razumovsky quartets were "not music"; Beethoven replied, "Oh, they are not for you, but for a later age!" His own temper made enemies: after Gottfried Weber's negative review he wrote a coarse retort, and he called the choirmaster Gebauer "peasant". Goethe, who met him at Teplitz in 1812, wrote that he was "an utterly untamed personality, who is not altogether wrong in finding the world detestable".

The sharpest conflict was over his nephew Karl. After his brother Kaspar died in 1815, Beethoven fought Kaspar's widow Johanna for custody. When he could not prove noble birth before the Landrechte, the case went in December 1818 to the civil magistrate, where he lost sole guardianship; he regained custody in 1820 after intensive legal struggles. Karl came to perceive his uncle's interference as overbearing, and in August 1826 he attempted suicide by shooting himself and survived.

Anton Schindler, who worked as his unpaid secretary from 1822 and in 1840 became one of his earliest and most influential, but not always reliable, biographers, claimed to have been in his circle since 1814; there is no evidence for this.
sections.last:
After his nephew's attempt on his life, Beethoven went with Karl to recuperate at Gneixendorf, where he completed the String Quartet in F major, Op. 135, and in November 1826 his final composition, a replacement finale for the Op. 130 quartet. He was already ill and depressed and quarrelled with his brother Johann, insisting that Johann make Karl his heir. On the return journey to Vienna in December 1826 illness struck again. Andreas Ignaz Wawruch noticed fever, jaundice and dropsy, and several operations were carried out to tap fluid from his abdomen. Karl left in January to join the army, and Beethoven wrote a will making him sole heir.

In January 1827 Dr. Malfatti treated him largely with alcohol. Old friends visited, and the Philharmonic Society of London sent £100 and Schotts a case of expensive wine. On 24 March he was given the Last Rites by a Roman Catholic priest and said to those present: "Plaudite, amici, comoedia finita est" ("Applaud, friends, the comedy is over"). When the wine arrived he whispered: "Pity – too late."

He died on 26 March 1827, aged 56. According to Anselm Hüttenbrenner, there was a flash of lightning and a clap of thunder at about 5 pm. An autopsy found significant liver damage, which could have been due to heavy alcohol consumption, and considerable dilation of the auditory and related nerves. His remains were exhumed for study in 1863 and moved in 1888.
sections.legacy:
Beethoven's career is conventionally divided into three periods. The historian William Drabkin notes that a writer proposed such a division as early as 1818, and that it became the convention among his biographers, though it omits the Bonn years and hides the uneven development of different kinds of work. The word "heroic" for the middle period has become increasingly controversial, since works such as the Pastoral Symphony are not easily called heroic. E. T. A. Hoffmann hailed him in 1810 as the greatest of three Romantic composers, ahead of Haydn and Mozart, and Harold C. Schonberg wrote that by the end he had become a composer "beyond time and space".

Alex Ross writes that Beethoven "molded entire institutions": the professional orchestra arose in large measure as a vehicle for the performance of his symphonies, and the art of conducting emerged in his wake. Schonberg holds that the Ninth Symphony most influenced Berlioz and Wagner, and Brahms's First Symphony quotes its "Ode to Joy" theme. His nine symphonies are the source of the superstition called the curse of the ninth.

Bonn unveiled the Beethoven Monument in August 1845, the first statue of a composer in Germany, and has held a Beethoven festival since 1845. Vienna honoured him with a statue in 1880. In 2001 his manuscript of the Ninth Symphony became the first musical score on UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

summary: Ludwig van Beethoven (1770–1827), born in Bonn, settled in Vienna in 1792 and became a leading pianist and composer. His hearing failed from about 1798, yet he wrote the Eroica, the Fifth and Ninth symphonies, the Missa solemnis and the late quartets, and his work shaped later composers and institutions.
references: Martin Cooper, Beethoven, The Last Decade 1817–1827 (Oxford University Press, 1970)
Lewis Lockwood, Beethoven: The Music and the Life (W.W. Norton, 2005)
Jan Swafford, Beethoven: Anguish and Triumph (Faber & Faber, 2014)
Alexander Wheelock Thayer, The Life of Ludwig van Beethoven (Beethoven Association, 1921)
notes: Birth: no documented date; the baptism of 17 December 1770 is certain and 16 December is the consensus. start is 1770, circa false.
The article's list of seven children says 'only Ludwig, the second-born, and two younger brothers survived'; kept as given.

Eroica: written 1803–04, premiere 'early 1805', published 1806; the 1805 event combines the premiere and the first Fidelio (November 1805). The article's intro says Fifth and Eroica premiered 1805 and 1808, with Eroica in 1805.

The article says in one place he began studying with Haydn 'under Haydn's direction' and counterpoint with Albrechtsberger from 1794; both given. Salieri instruction 'until at least 1802, possibly 1809' left out.

Left out: the Immortal Beloved debate and the proposals to Therese Malfatti, Antonie Brentano's son (speculation), prostitution remark, the Goethe letters beyond the 1812 quotation, pianos, Alex Ross's recording-technology claim, Hoffmann's review of the Fifth in detail, 'greatest composer' claims, the literary, popular-culture and Voyager items.

The Karl/Johanna dispute: the article gives only Beethoven's side of custody in detail (and says Johanna was his 'old enemy' in the death scene); Karl's view is given as 'perceived as overbearing'. Johanna's own account is not in the article.
The deathbed quotation 'Plaudite, amici' is dated 24 March by the article; the Last Rites the same day.
In 'opponents', the coarse retort to Weber is described, not quoted. The 'Geh! Bauer' remark is rendered as 'peasant' for Gebauer.
Possible garble: the article's 'Johann's's' and 'inwas unveiled' are typos; the Bonn Monument date (August 1845) is taken as given. Hammerklavier premiere by Liszt in 1836 left out.
Role fact: 'composer in residence at the Theater an der Wien' is from 1803 (appointment) and its end 'early 1804' is from the termination of his position; both from the article.
